pages.title: UN's relevance, goals and overall assessment
pages.summary: Lecture 23 (26/04/2017) lists questions on the UN's relevance, areas of reform, UNSC reform and the ICJ. Quoting Dag Hammarskjold that the UN exists to prevent hell, it lists the Charter Preamble goals (ending war, fundamental rights, justice and international law, social progress) and judges performance unsatisfactory though things would be worse without the UN.

pages.title: Opinions on UN; paralysis and need for UN
pages.summary: Gareth Evans calls the Security Council a prisoner of great power manoeuvring, the General Assembly empty rhetoric, ECOSOC dysfunctional and the Secretariat inefficient. Yet Ban Ki-moon says the world needs more UN, global governance is a necessity, the UN was paralysed in the Cold War, and the Council is now divided between P3 and P2.

pages.title: Abolish or reform UN; reforms on principles
pages.summary: Abolishing the UN is pointless so reform is needed, but prospects are very dim as the General Assembly failed to agree on reforms even at the 70th anniversary. Proposed reforms are rethinking Article 2(7) non-intervention in light of responsibility to protect, dropping the 'enemy states' reference as Germany and Japan seek permanent seats, and better General Assembly-UNSC coordination.

pages.title: UNSC, Trusteeship Council and ECOSOC reform
pages.summary: Suggests the General Assembly be able to override a veto by special majority. UNSC reform needs transparency (Hardeep Puri's book on the Council's internal chaos), veto reform and membership reform, while the Trusteeship Council should be abolished or given the global commons and ECOSOC streamlined.

pages.title: Secretariat, funding, peacekeeping; Article 108 begins
pages.summary: The Secretariat needs right-sizing and equitable distribution as western countries dominate, and funding is weak because dues are paid late and the USA is a frequent defaulter, with a Tobin tax suggested. Peacekeeping is losing support and lacks standby forces; reform prospects are next to impossible because Article 108 needs a two-thirds General Assembly resolution without a P5 veto.

pages.title: Article 108 ratification; Truman's concluding quote
pages.summary: After the resolution passes, amendments must be ratified by member states under their domestic processes. The conclusion says reform will not come while nations pursue narrow national interest, so failure is ours not the UN's, supported by Truman's quote that the UN is a creation of its member states.

pages.title: UNSC decision making and the veto problem
pages.summary: Procedural matters need the affirmative vote of any 9 of 15 members, while substantive matters need 9 votes with no P5 veto. The veto is the main reason the UN fails to act, since one permanent member can block action despite overwhelming General Assembly support, and it was introduced at the Soviet Union's insistence.

pages.title: Veto options, membership expansion and aspirants
pages.summary: Veto options are to abolish it (no permanent member will agree), restrict it to core national interest, or give the General Assembly overriding power. The Council had 5 permanent and 6 non-permanent members when the Assembly had 51, got 4 more non-permanent seats in 1963 and has not expanded since, leaving Europe over-represented; aspirants include the G4, African Union and L69.

pages.title: OIC claim, coffee club and reform efforts
pages.summary: The OIC also seeks representation, and countries agree on reform but not on criteria, candidates or procedure. Regional rivals Pakistan, Mexico, Italy and South Korea formed the 12-member coffee club against the G4 and its Uniting for Consensus resolution, in contrast to the G4's Article 108 majority route; reform efforts since 1992 include Kofi Annan's 2002 agenda.

pages.title: Reform documents; India's UNSC ambition
pages.summary: Lists reform documents: the Millennium Declaration 2000, the 2004 High-level Panel report and In Larger Freedom (2005). A permanent seat is India's ultimate diplomatic dream and an ambition since Nehru, formally presented in 1972 and pursued seriously since 1992, and India objected when the USA backed Germany and Japan, saying the seat is not for sale.

pages.title: India's UNSC credentials and strategies
pages.summary: India cites its second-largest population, seventh-largest size and economy, peacekeeping contribution, democracy, civilisation, professional diplomats and seven terms as non-permanent member. Strategies tried are going alone, the G4 coalition (counterproductive), a G4 offer of no veto for 15 years to the coffee club, while the African Union's Ezulwini consensus insists on veto.

pages.title: More strategies, prospects, scholars' views
pages.summary: India also works with key groups, P5 states and developing countries, and cites nuclear weapons and the third-largest military. The General Assembly discussion on 7 November 2016 reached no conclusion and P5 stands are ambiguous, with views from Ramachandra Guha, Kishor Manubhai and C. Raja Mohan.

pages.title: Scholars' views; Kofi Annan formula; ICJ assignment
pages.summary: Shamsaran and Ramesh Thakur add views, and the notes record that reform is a top priority with China not publicly opposed. Kofi Annan's formula adds 9 members without veto, in Model A as G4 plus 2 African Union permanent seats and 3 non-permanent (which India supported), in Model B as 8 semi-permanent seats and 1 non-permanent (which Pakistan supports); assignments are on the ICJ.

pages.title: ICJ composition and jurisdiction
pages.summary: The ICJ is the only UN body inherited directly from the League of Nations, with 15 judges serving 9-year terms, one-third retiring every 3 years and elected by the General Assembly and UNSC. It has contentious jurisdiction (consent of parties), advisory jurisdiction and optional compulsory jurisdiction, which India accepted in 1974.

pages.title: India's ICJ exceptions; WTO history
pages.summary: India does not accept compulsory jurisdiction for disputes involving Commonwealth members or past members, or those relating to hostilities or armed conflict in self-defence. WTO, the third pillar of the US-conceived liberal economic order, replaced the failed ITO and GATT, began on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round using the Dunkel Draft, is based in Geneva, and was joined by developing countries after 1980s crises.

pages.title: Near-empty page pointing to page 136
pages.summary: Carries only a pointer reading 'For page 136', with no other notes.

flashcards.front: What objectives does the Preamble of the UN Charter set out?
flashcards.back: To save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, reaffirm faith in fundamental rights and human dignity, strengthen conditions for justice and respect for international law, and promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom.

flashcards.front: How does Gareth Evans assess the main organs of the UN?
flashcards.back: He says no other organisation embodies so many dreams and frustrations: the Security Council is a prisoner of great power manoeuvring, the General Assembly a theatre of empty rhetoric, ECOSOC dysfunctional and irrelevant, and the Secretariat full of inefficient individuals.

flashcards.front: Which reforms of UN principles are proposed in the notes?
flashcards.back: Article 2(7) bars intervention in domestic affairs under a Westphalian order, so post-Cold War needs call for more intervention, as with responsibility to protect. The Charter's 'enemy states' reference is anachronistic since Germany and Japan now seek permanent seats.

flashcards.front: Why are reforms under Article 108 of the UN Charter called next to impossible?
flashcards.back: An amendment needs a General Assembly resolution passed by two-thirds of members, provided no P5 member uses its veto. The amendment must then be ratified by member states through their domestic processes.

flashcards.front: How does the UNSC vote on procedural and substantive matters, and why is the veto a problem?
flashcards.back: Procedural matters need the affirmative vote of any 9 members, and substantive matters need 9 of 15 with no P5 veto. A single permanent member can block action despite overwhelming General Assembly support, and the veto was introduced at the Soviet Union's insistence.

flashcards.front: How has UNSC membership changed since 1945, and what imbalance remains?
flashcards.back: It began with 5 permanent and 6 non-permanent members when the General Assembly had 51, and 4 non-permanent seats were added in 1963 when it had 113, with no expansion since. Europe is over-represented, Asia under-represented, and Latin America and Africa not represented.

flashcards.front: Who are the aspirants for permanent UNSC seats, and what is the coffee club?
flashcards.back: Aspirants are the G4 (India, Japan, Brazil, Germany), the African Union (two seats, no consensus on candidates), the L69 group and the OIC. The coffee club of Pakistan, Mexico, Italy, South Korea and others opposes the G4 through the Uniting for Consensus resolution.

flashcards.front: What credentials does India cite for a permanent seat in the UNSC?
flashcards.back: Second-largest population, seventh-largest size and economy, a major UN peacekeeping contribution, a functioning democracy and civilisational diversity, professional diplomats, and seven terms as non-permanent member with overwhelming support.

flashcards.front: What are the two models in Kofi Annan's formula for expanding the UNSC?
flashcards.back: Both add 9 members to the 15 with no veto for new members. Model A gives permanent seats to the G4 plus 2 African Union members and adds 3 non-permanent seats, and India supported it; Model B adds 8 semi-permanent seats for 4 years and 1 non-permanent seat, and Pakistan supports it.

flashcards.front: Distinguish the contentious, advisory and compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ.
flashcards.back: Contentious jurisdiction needs the consent of the parties, and advisory jurisdiction lets the ICJ advise all UN bodies including the UNSC and General Assembly. Compulsory jurisdiction, if adopted, removes the need for prior consent but does not itself make the verdict binding, and India accepted it in 1974.

answers.question: Discuss the areas in which UN reform is needed and why the prospects of reform are considered dim.
answers.intro: The UN was created to prevent the world becoming hell, yet its performance on core goals is judged unsatisfactory. The notes reject abolition, argue for reform to improve efficiency, representativeness and legitimacy, but judge reform prospects very dim.
body: Principles and organs: Article 2(7) bars intervention in domestic affairs, yet post-Cold War needs, as with responsibility to protect, demand more; 'enemy states' references are anachronistic; the Trusteeship Council should be abolished or given the global commons; ECOSOC needs streamlining.

Security Council: it needs transparency (Hardeep Puri's account of internal chaos), veto reform, including General Assembly override by special majority, and wider membership, since Europe is over-represented while Africa and Latin America are not represented.

Secretariat, funding and peacekeeping: right-size the bureaucracy and end western dominance; reduce dependence on late dues, including frequent US default, through independent revenue such as a Tobin tax; address falling interest in dangerous peacekeeping without standby forces.

Why prospects are dim: Article 108 needs a two-thirds General Assembly vote with no P5 veto, then domestic ratification by member states; the General Assembly failed to agree reforms even at the 70th anniversary, and states pursue narrow national interest.
answers.conclusion: Reform is necessary but blocked by the rigid amendment process and narrow national interests. As Truman said, the UN is a creation of its member states, so its success depends on their willingness to fulfil their duties.

answers.question: Examine India's case for a permanent seat in the UN Security Council and the obstacles to reform.
answers.intro: A permanent UNSC seat is described as India's ultimate diplomatic dream, an ambition since Nehru. India presses a broad case of credentials, but divided aspirants, P5 ambiguity and a rigid Charter process have kept the seat out of reach.
body: Credentials: second-largest population, seventh-largest size and economy, a major peacekeeping contribution, a functioning democracy with civilisational diversity, professional diplomats and seven terms as non-permanent member with overwhelming support; India also cites nuclear weapons and the third-largest military.

Strategies: India first presented its case formally in 1972 and pressed seriously from 1992; it tried going alone, then the G4 coalition, which proved counterproductive, and it objected when the USA backed Germany and Japan, saying the seat is not for sale.

Obstacles: no consensus on criteria, candidates or procedure; the coffee club (Pakistan, Mexico, Italy, South Korea and others) opposes the G4 through Uniting for Consensus; the G4 offered to forgo veto for 15 years, but the African Union's Ezulwini consensus insists on it.

Prospects: the General Assembly's 7 November 2016 discussion reached no conclusion; the USA gave oral support, Russia and China remain ambiguous and may favour India without veto; Ramachandra Guha urges internal development and C. Raja Mohan warns against being bargained by western countries.
answers.conclusion: India's case rests on size, democracy and contribution, but reform depends on consensus among rival aspirants and the P5. A realistic strategy combines coalition-building, careful diplomacy with the P5 and, as scholars advise, real internal strength.
